title.zh: 长出棉花般柔软楼梯的云中城堡
title.en: The Cloud-Castle That Grew Cotton-Soft Stairs

content:
在高高的天上，天空呼吸得又慢又蓝，  
轻飘飘的风儿哼着柔软又真诚的摇篮曲。  
那儿浮着一座城堡——不是石头造的，也不是木头搭的，  
而是用最最蓬松的云朵，一缕一缕纺出来的。  

它的塔尖弯弯的，像打了个懒懒的哈欠，  
它的尖顶闪着晨光，亮晶晶的，  
它的墙闪闪发亮，又淡又亮，  
像温热的牛奶上撒了一层糖霜。  

没人用锤子、钉子把它敲敲打打建起来，  
没有梯子能爬上去，也没有绳子够得到它。  
它每天悠悠地飘呀飘，乘着温柔的风，  
身后留下一道道银色的、轻轻的痕迹。  

在下面，一个绿油油的山谷里，  
雏菊点着头，小溪哗啦啦唱着干净的歌，  
住着一个小女孩，名叫莉拉，她穿着一件  
星星缝成的小衬衫，头发软软的，像海边的草。  
每天傍晚，当暮色把山丘染成深深的金黄，  
莉拉就会坐在野紫罗兰睡觉的地方，  
抬起小下巴，静静地看呀看——  
看着云朵城堡慢慢飘过，总也不远，  
可也……从没真的靠近过。  

有一个星期二，蒲公英花低着头，空气里飘着雨后薄荷的清香，  
莉拉忽然发现了一件新东西——一件温柔又特别的东西。  
一根细细的、白白的线，从西边塔楼的檐角垂下来，  
轻轻晃呀晃，像一朵蒲公英的种子，被风儿悄悄逗着玩。  

莉拉伸出小手。  
那根线碰到了她的指尖——暖暖的，不凉，  
软软的，像小猫耳朵，像露水沾在羊毛上。  
它没有断开，也没有变淡。  
它就停在那里——安安静静，柔柔的，一点也不害怕。  

莉拉笑了。  
那根线，就长了一点。  

不快，也不响。  
就慢慢地，一寸，又一寸，  
等在心跳之间的安静里，等在叹气之间的平和里，  
像时间在安静的天空下，轻轻叠起自己。  

很快，第二根线来了——接着是第三根、第四根——  
全都缠在一起，还是那么柔软，  
可现在变得更粗了，更圆润了，更饱满啦，  
就像梦里的人，亲手 spun出的棉花糖。  

它们自己织成了一架楼梯——啊，多奇妙的楼梯呀！  
宽宽的，刚好够两只光脚丫并排走，  
台阶软乎乎的，像棉花糖，又厚又蓬松，  
每一阶都托着一声轻叹，每一步都裹着睡意。  

没有铁做的扶手，也没有高高的栏杆——  
只有云朵的光 puff puff 地浮着，软软的，像一句  
睡前的悄悄话，轻轻的，清清楚楚：  
“上来吧，小宝贝，什么也不用怕。”  

莉拉脱下鞋子——两只小小的蓝布鞋，  
把一只小脚丫，轻轻地、软软地，放在第一阶上。  
台阶微微陷下去一点点，像雨水里的青苔，  
然后稳稳地托住了她，像爱一样，像名字一样，  
被温柔地、慢慢地叫出来，在一天快要结束的时候，  
那时影子变长了，烦心事也悄悄飘走了。  

她抬起另一只脚——轻得像一片羽毛——  
就这样站着，安安静静的，在暖暖的金色阳光里。  
楼梯在她身后缓缓升起，一条柔和的白色斜坡，  
而云朵城堡就在前面等着——不着急，不盼望，  
不催促，不强求——只是敞开着，宽宽的，暖暖的，  
窗户像一声声轻叹，门也跟着轻轻叹息。  

一只知更鸟落在莉拉肩膀上，羽毛软软的，一动不动，  
胸口一起一伏，慢慢、暖暖地跳着。  
一只小瓢虫停在她的膝盖上，  
红得像一颗小浆果，静得像大海，  
在黄昏时分安安静静躺着，连涟漪都不再荡漾。  
连风也停下了——就停在山坡上，轻轻歇了一会儿。  

莉拉抬起头——不高，也不远——  
刚刚好，能看到城堡那双温柔的眼睛，  
其实是一扇圆圆的、大大的、清亮的窗，  
框着一片蓝天，还有一只纯白的小鹿，  
它眨了一下眼睛，慢得像花瓣飘落，  
长长的睫毛像蒲公英绒毛，  
然后它转过身，轻轻走出了云朵的小镇，  
走进雾里——那里，光好像正悄悄开花，  
像阳光洒进厨房时，刚出炉的面包香。  

莉拉深深吸了一口气。  
空气尝起来，有三叶草的味道，有安静的味道，有家的味道。  
她的眼皮越来越沉——不是累，而是“被懂得”的感觉，  
像妈妈把你的小被子掖得严严实实，你心里暖暖的、妥妥的。  

楼梯不着急。  
城堡也不呼唤。  
整个世界屏住了呼吸——让温柔，轻轻落下，  
像樱桃树的花瓣，慢悠悠、静悄悄；  
像月光，悄悄聚在最柔软的草尖上。  

莉拉还站在那儿，一只脚踩在楼梯上，  
一只脚踏在地上，知更鸟就在她肩头，  
她心里有什么东西——小小的、暖暖的、深深的——  
开始慢慢舒展开来……像一个要藏起来的小秘密……  
像一个等了很久的愿望……像一种悄悄生长的感觉……  
不吵，不猛，只是……轻轻地，知道自己的存在。  

风又轻轻吹了起来——那么轻，那么低——  
带来一个只有做梦的孩子才听得见的声音：  
一声哼唱，  

像蒲公英的绒毛和月光一起纺成的摇篮曲。  
它升起来了——不是从城堡里，也不是从天空中，  
而是从莉拉呼出的气息和云朵柔软的弧线之间，轻轻浮起。  
她把手指轻轻停在楼梯边缘，那棉花糖一样软的台阶，  
也轻轻“呼”地回应她——暖暖的一声叹息，  
像冬天早晨，从抽屉里抽出一件晒过太阳的毛衣。  

她慢慢地，抬起一只光脚丫——脚趾头轻轻翘起来，越过台阶边缘——  
然后，迈了上去。  

没有吱呀声，也没有晃动，只有一声轻轻的“嘘——”，  
仿佛这朵云，一直都在等这一刻，等她这轻轻的重量。  
第二级台阶，稳稳地托住她的另一只脚，无声无息。  
接着是第三级——城堡也微微朝她靠过来一点点，  
塔尖像刚睡醒的小猫，在阳光里伸个懒腰。  
小小的窗户，一扇一扇睁开了——不是玻璃做的，  
而是像液态的星光，每扇窗里，都映着一个安静的画面：  
莉拉笑着；莉拉眨着眼睛；莉拉的头发像被风吹散的蒲公英，  
她的睡衣上，还沾着一点点睡意的碎屑。  

她没有跑着爬。她是一步一步，慢慢爬的，  
像一只一只数萤火虫，或者用指尖一圈一圈描茶杯的边。  
每迈上一级，空气就更柔软一点——不是变冷，也不是变热，  
而是变得更“满”了，仿佛呼吸一下子轻松了，更深了，  
像夏天午后，躺在高高的草丛里，一动不动。  
几缕云丝轻轻飘下来，蹭蹭她的鼻子——  
还不至于打喷嚏，只让她忍不住咯咯笑，  
可那笑声太小啦，还没离开嘴唇，就变成一个哈欠。  

爬到一半，她停下来歇一歇。  
往下看，整个世界都浸在薄暮的宁静里：屋顶披着天鹅绒般的影子，  
树站得像安静的哨兵，她家后院的小篱笆，  
看起来像铅笔画出来的一条线——轻轻的，包容的，暂时的。  
往前看，城堡那扇大大的、圆圆的门洞，正微微发亮，  
不是亮光，而是“邀请”。它不发光，它“往里发光”，  
像把海螺贴在耳边听到的声音——暖暖的，嗡嗡的，  
盛满了只有心才记得的安静音乐。  

一个声音来了——没有词语，只有感觉，  
像小时候被人轻轻摇着哄睡的记忆：  
“你不用找钥匙。你早就握着门闩啦。”  

莉拉摸摸自己的胸口，那里，心跳得又慢又稳，  
像一个裹着青苔的鼓。然后她明白了：  
这楼梯，不是通向城堡的路，  
而是穿过——穿过担心，穿过着急，  
穿过那些关灯以后，像飞蛾一样扑在窗玻璃上的“要是……怎么办？”  
每一步，都悄悄融化掉一个，像糖融进温热的牛奶里。  

当她走到最顶端，门洞无声地打开了。  
里面没有大厅，也没有王座，  
只有一个又大又圆的房间——地板是雾织成的丝，  
挂着会飘的灯笼，形状像卷起来的蕨类叶子。  
房间中央，是一个矮矮的、软软的小窝，  
堆满了云朵绒和暮蓝色天鹅绒做的靠枕。  
旁边，放在一道由凝固的月光雕成的架子上，  
放着一块小小的、滑溜溜的石头——摸起来暖暖的，  
灰灰白白的纹路，温柔极了，大小刚刚好，  
刚好能放进她小小的手心里。  

一个声音轻轻擦过她的耳朵，软得像睫毛落下来：  
“这是你的石头。它装着你的平静。  
当世界变得太吵，就把它捧在手心，  
深呼吸，记住——楼梯是怎么长出来的？  
不是因为你用力推，而是因为你停了下来……  
然后，相信了那份柔软。”  

莉拉拿起那块石头。它乖乖躺在她掌心里。  
她蜷进靠枕堆里，把膝盖收起来，  
把最软的那个枕头垫在脸颊底下。  
灯笼慢慢暗下去——不是变黑，而是变成更深的金色，  
像蜂蜜静静沉在玻璃罐底。  
那声哼唱，轻轻变响了，像一条熟悉的旧毯子，  
把她轻轻裹住，把她的念头，一个一个，  
缝成一片片安静。她的手指松开了，  
肩膀沉下去了，眼皮重得像合拢的花瓣，  
开始慢慢、甜甜地，往下坠……  

城堡外面，星星悄悄凑近了。  
风也安静了。连蟋蟀都把歌声放轻了，  
只剩下一两声慵懒的“唧——”，  
然后，静下来了，只听见莉拉的呼吸声，  
轻轻的、慢慢的：呼……吸……呼……吸……  
像海浪一遍遍抚平岸边的小石子，  
而那片海滩，只有她一个人能看见。  

当她最后一个念头飘走——不是消失了，  
而是像糖融进温热的牛奶里，轻轻化开了——  
她感觉到，云朵城堡在她身下，也轻轻叹了口气，  
不是因为费力，而是因为深深的、梦里的满足。  
它在天空里，又轻轻往下沉了一点点，  
像妈妈抱着一个叹息那样，把她稳稳地抱在怀里。  

她的小手，还握着那块石头，一动不动。  
她的呼吸更深了。她的睫毛，像小蝴蝶翅膀，  
轻轻停在脸颊上。而远远的、远远的山脚下，  
一朵夜来香，悄悄绽开，把它的甜香，  
送进空气里——只是整首世界摇篮曲里，  
一个小小的、完美的音符，  
轻柔、缓慢、笃定……  

……只为她。  

……就在此刻。
contentEn:
High up where the sky breathes slow and blue,  
Where wisps of wind hum lullabies soft and true,  
There floated a castle—not stone, not wood—  
But spun from the fluffiest cloud that ever could.  

Its towers curled like sleepy sighs,  
Its turrets gleamed with morning’s light,  
And its walls shimmered, pale and bright,  
Like sugar-dust on warm milk-white.  

No one built it with hammer or nail,  
No ladder reached it, no rope could scale.  
It drifted each day on a breeze so kind,  
Leaving trails of silver behind.  

Down below, in a valley of green,  
Where daisies nodded and brooks babbled clean,  
Lived a small child named Lila, who wore  
A shirt stitched with stars and hair soft as shore-grass.  
Each evening, when dusk painted hills gold and deep,  
Lila would sit where the wild violets sleep,  
Tilt her chin up, and watch—just watch—  
As the Cloud-Castle sailed by, never out of reach…  
but never quite near, either.  

One Tuesday, when buttercups bowed and the air smelled of rain-washed mint,  
Lila noticed something new—something tender, distinct.  
A thread, thin and white, hung down from the west tower’s rim,  
Swaying like a dandelion seed caught on a whim.  

She held out her hand.  
The thread touched her fingertip—warm, not cool,  
Soft as kitten-ear, soft as dew on a wool.  
It didn’t snap. It didn’t fade.  
It stayed—gentle, quiet, unafraid.  

Lila smiled.  
And the thread grew.  

Not fast. Not loud.  
Just one slow inch, then another, allowed  
By the hush between heartbeats, the calm between sighs,  
Like time folding softly beneath quiet skies.  

Soon, a second thread joined it—then three, then four—  
All twisting together, soft as before,  
But now thicker, plumper, round and grand,  
Like spun sugar spun by a dreamer’s hand.  

They wove themselves into a stair—oh, what a stair!  
Wide enough for two bare feet to share,  
With steps like marshmallows, pillowy and deep,  
Each one holding a sigh, each one wrapped in sleep.  

No railings of iron, no banisters tall—  
Just puffs of cloud-light, soft as a call  
Whispered at bedtime, low and clear:  
*“Step up, little one. There’s nothing to fear.”*  

Lila took off her shoes—two small things of blue cloth—  
And placed one foot on the first step, both slow and both soft.  
It gave just a little, like moss under rain,  
Then held her quite steady, like love, like a name  
Said slowly and fondly at close of the day,  
When shadows grow longer and worries drift away.  

She lifted her other foot—light as a feather—  
And stood there, quite still, in the warm, golden weather.  
The stair rose behind her, a gentle, white slope,  
While the Cloud-Castle waited—no hurry, no hope,  
No rush, no demand—just open and wide,  
With windows like sighs, and doors that sighed *inside*.  

A robin alighted on Lila’s shoulder, soft-feathered and still,  
Its chest rising slow with a quiet, warm thrill.  
A ladybug landed upon her knee,  
Red as a berry, calm as the sea  
When it rests at twilight, all ripples gone still.  
Even the breeze paused—just paused—on the hill.  

Lila looked up—not too far, not too high—  
Just enough to see the castle’s soft eye  
(Which was really a window, round, wide, and clear,  
Framing sky-blue and a single white deer  
That blinked once, so slowly, with lashes like down,  
Then turned, and walked softly out of the town  
Of clouds—into mist—where the light seemed to bloom  
Like the scent of warm bread in a sunlit room).  

Lila breathed in.  
The air tasted like clover and quiet and home.  
Her eyelids grew heavy—not tired, but *known*,  
Like a blanket tucked tight when you’re safe in your own.  

The stairs did not hurry.  
The castle did not call.  
The world held its breath—and let kindness fall  
Like petals from cherry trees, slow and serene,  
Like moonlight that pools where the softest grass leans.  

And Lila, still standing, one foot on the stair,  
One foot on the earth, with the robin right there,  
Felt something inside her—small, warm, and deep—  
Begin to unfurl… like a secret to keep…  
like a wish that had waited… like something that grows…  
not loud, not sudden… but *softly*, and *knows*.  

The breeze stirred again—so gentle, so low—  
And carried a sound only dreamers can know:  
A hum, like

a lullaby spun from dandelion fluff and moonlight.  
It rose—not from the castle, not from the sky—but from the very air between Lila’s breath and the cloud’s soft curve. She held her fingers just shy of the stair’s edge, and the cotton-soft step *breathed* back—a sigh of warmth, like sun-warmed wool pulled from a drawer on a winter morning.  

Slowly, she lifted one bare foot—her toes curling over the edge—and stepped up.  

No creak. No wobble. Just a quiet *hush*, as if the cloud had been waiting all along for this exact weight, this exact moment. The second step rose beneath her other foot, seamless, silent. Then the third—and with it, the castle leaned just a little closer, its turrets puffing like sleepy kittens stretching in sunbeams. Tiny windows blinked open—not with glass, but with pools of liquid starlight, each holding its own quiet reflection: Lila, smiling; Lila, blinking; Lila, with hair like wind-tossed thistledown and pajamas dusted with sleep-dust.  

She didn’t climb fast. She climbed *slowly*, like counting fireflies one by one, or tracing the rim of a teacup with a fingertip. With each step, the air grew softer—not cooler, not warmer, but *fuller*, as if breathing had become easier, deeper, like lying in tall grass on a still summer afternoon. A few stray cloud-threads drifted down, tickling her nose—not enough to sneeze, just enough to make her giggle, a sound so small it turned into a yawn before it left her lips.  

Halfway up, she paused. Below, the world was wrapped in twilight hush: rooftops wore velvet shadows, trees stood like quiet sentinels, and her own backyard fence looked like a line drawn in pencil—gentle, forgiving, temporary. Up ahead, the castle’s great arched doorway shimmered, not with light, but with *invitation*. It didn’t glow. It *glowed inward*, like the inside of a seashell held to the ear—warm, humming, full of quiet music only the heart remembers.  

A voice came—not with words, but with feeling, like the memory of being rocked:  
*You don’t need a key. You already hold the latch.*  

Lila touched her chest, where her heart beat slow and steady, like a drum wrapped in moss. And then she understood: the stairs weren’t leading *to* the castle. They were leading *through*—through worry, through hurry, through all the “what-ifs” that sometimes buzzed like moths at the windowpane after lights-out. Each step dissolved one, softly, like sugar in warm milk.  

When she reached the top, the doorway opened without sound. Inside wasn’t a hall or a throne room, but a single, wide, round room—floored in spun-silk mist, lit by floating lanterns shaped like curled ferns. In the center sat a low, cushioned nook, piled high with pillows made of cloud-down and twilight-blue velvet. And beside it, resting on a shelf carved from solidified moonbeam, stood a small, smooth stone—warm to the touch, striped in gentle grays and creams, exactly the size of her small palm.  

A whisper brushed her ear, soft as eyelash-fall:  
*This is your stone. It holds your calm. When the world feels too loud, hold it. Breathe. Remember how the stairs grew—not because you pushed, but because you paused… and trusted the soft.*  

Lila picked up the stone. It fit perfectly. She curled onto the cushions, tucking her knees, pulling the softest pillow beneath her cheek. The lanterns dimmed—not into dark, but into deeper gold, like honey settling in a jar. The hum swelled gently, wrapping around her like a well-loved blanket, stitching her thoughts together, one by one, into quiet. Her fingers uncurled. Her shoulders sank. Her eyelids, heavy as folded petals, began their slow, sweet descent.  

Outside the castle, the stars leaned in. The breeze stilled. Even the crickets softened their song to a single, drowsy chirp—then another—then silence, broken only by the soft, slow rhythm of Lila’s breathing: in… out… in… out… like waves smoothing pebbles on a shore no one else could see.  

And as her last thought floated away—not vanishing, but dissolving, like sugar in warm milk—she felt the cloud-castle sigh beneath her, not with effort, but with deep, dreamy contentment. It settled, just a little lower in the sky, cradling her like a mother cradling a sigh.  

Her hand, still holding the stone, grew still. Her breath deepened. Her lashes rested like moth-wings on her cheeks. And somewhere, far below, a night-blooming jasmine released its sweetness into the air—just one small, perfect note in the lullaby the whole world was singing, soft and slow and sure…  

…just for her.  

Just for now
